## Claim + dispatch — **design only**, no implementation, no follow-up cards filed

- **Session**: `session_01APWX2AwT3a4xDcjPCe8bk4` (`os-sam`, `domain:services` execution seat)
- **Branch**: `claude/issue-11633-cross-request-cache-design` (claim marker; ⛔ no PR expected unless the design turns out ADR-class)
- **Worktree**: `../objectstack-11633-design` (per-repo; ⛔ never the shared checkout; ⛔ never `git stash`)
- **Container & model**: `claude-opus-5` — no path-derived tier mandate (a design deliverable touches no mandated surface), and the **measured quota exemption** applies this round regardless: a dev on this lane terminated at ~11:50Z with `You've reached your Fable 5 limit`, so fable-tier execution is not reliably available (fable unavailable ⇒ opus, never lower).
- `pm:queue` → `pm:dispatched`

Honouring this card's own discipline: the deliverable is the **design document**, and 「Implementation is dispatched as follow-up cards against the approved design, not as riders on this one.」 ⛔ No product code. ⛔ No implementation. ⛔ No follow-up cards filed — the dev **proposes** the split; filing waits on your acceptance.

⚠️ **If the design is ADR-class**: `docs/adr/**` is a **governed surface** — draft PR, **human merge**. ⛔ This seat never flips ready, never arms auto-merge and never merges a governed surface, whatever the review says.

## The framing the dev is held to, verbatim from the card

> Caching session and authorization state is **a security change wearing a performance costume** — a stale grants cache is a privilege-escalation window (a permission revoked at T honoured until TTL expiry).

The ruled direction is a **fence, not a starting point**: write-invalidation primary, short TTL as a fallback *bound* rather than the mechanism, configurable down to zero, low-sensitivity legs first, multi-node story stated explicitly. ⛔ A deviation comes back as a **fork for you to rule on**, never as a quiet design choice.

## ⭐ Two authorization surfaces this design sits on top of are MOVING right now

The dev could not know this from the card, so it has been told:

- **#10348** (ruled option C, dispatched this round, Clause-② / `needs:contract-review`): the two stray `plugin-auth` platform-admin judges are deleted and both call sites ask `core/security/resolve-authz-context.ts`. ⇒ **The thing a grants cache would cache is being consolidated to one site as we speak.** Design for the post-C single derivation point.
- **#11663** (`priority:p0`, design delivered, now `needs-user-decision`): platform-admin re-anchors onto env-configured verified emails, retiring the org-less row anchor. ⇒ **Part of "grants" may stop being a row read at all.** A cache keyed on grant rows would be caching something the re-anchor removes.

The dev is instructed to state explicitly which parts of its cache design depend on either landing, rather than silently assuming today's shape — the same coupling disclosure #11663's designer was held to.

## Fences

⛔ **Zero `packages/spec` ownership** — a spec change is named as a spec-seat leg, never taken. ⛔ **cloud#1521 / cloud#1518 are NOT reachable from this session** (repo scope is `objectstack-ai/objectstack`): reason only from what this card records, and **mark that leg NOT MEASURED** rather than inferring it. ⛔ Never edit `content/docs/releases/`, `.claude/**`, `skills/**`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`.

⛔ **Disclosure discipline**: the design describes an escalation *window* class. Public text carries the design and its reasoning — **no reproduction recipe** for exploiting a stale cache.

# Design — cross-request caching for the authenticated request path (tranche 2)

**Form chosen: this issue comment, not an ADR — deliberately, and with a proposal attached.**
See §9. **Measurement base:** every code claim below was read on a full (non-shallow) worktree
cut from `origin/main` at **`992161b728`**; `origin/main` has since moved one commit
(`88b9d749a1`, plugin-audit `sys_activity` vocabulary) which touches none of the files cited.
Claims carried from the card's 2026-08-21 trace rather than re-measured are marked
**NOT MEASURED** inline.

---

## 0. The frame, and what it changes about the shape of the answer

The card's framing is that this is a security change wearing a performance costume. Taken
seriously, it changes the *unit of design*. The unit is not "a cache". The unit is:

> **A cached answer together with the declared contract that says when it stops being an answer.**

So the design rule this document proposes, and which every leg below is written against:

> **No authorization answer may be cached unless (a) every write that can change it passes a
> seam this process observes, and (b) a TTL bounds the case where (a) fails. Both. Always.
> Neither alone is a design.**

(a) alone fails on the writer this process cannot see — another node, a migration, a DBA.
(b) alone is the timer the card's ruling already refuses. The interesting content of this
document is mostly in the places where (a) turns out to be *cheaper and stronger than expected*,
and in three places where (a) is **not derivable** and the design has to say so out loud.

---

## 1. What a request actually pays today — re-measured on `992161b728`

Tranches 1 and 1b have landed since the card's trace, so the numbers moved. Measured by reading
the code, not by reasoning from the card:

| leg | site | reads today | legs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** session | better-auth `findSession` | `sys_session` + `sys_user` — **NOT MEASURED** this round (carried from the card's 2026-08-21 rig trace); the *mechanism* was re-verified (§5) | 1–2 |
| **A** session | `customSession` callback, `auth-manager.ts:3061` | `sys_user_permission_set {user_id} limit 50`, `sys_permission_set {} limit 50` (**no `where` — full page**), `sys_member {user_id, organization_id} limit 5`; plus `findOne sys_session` when idle/absolute controls are on | 3+ |
| **B** grants | `resolveUserAuthzGrants`, `resolve-authz-context.ts:319` | 8 reads in **4 waves** post-#10825: wave 1 = `Promise.all` over `sys_user`(conditional) + `sys_member{user_id}` + `sys_user_position` + `sys_member{organization_id} limit 1000` + `sys_user_permission_set`; then `sys_position` → `sys_position_permission_set` → `sys_permission_set` sequentially | 4 |
| **C** localization | `resolveLocalizationContext`, `:726` | 1 `settings.getMany('localization', [timezone, locale, currency])` → 1 `loadRows` (all three keys are tenant/global scope, so the two-group split collapses to one) | 1 |
| **D** metadata | `getMetaItems`, `protocol.ts:5992`, per `enforceApiAccess` | `queryByOrg(null)` **then** `queryByOrg(orgId)`, each with an **alt-type retry when the first returns empty** ⇒ 2–4 reads, and the two `queryByOrg` calls are *awaited in sequence* | ≥2 |

Two things worth pulling out of that table before the design starts:

- **Leg D's cost is concentrated in the empty case.** The alt-type retry fires *because* the
  first read returned nothing, so an app whose objects are all code-authored (no overlay rows)
  pays the doubled read on **every** request. Most of leg D's win is negative caching.
- **Leg C is already one query.** #10826 did that. Leg C is now worth caching for the *round
  trip*, not for the query count — which matters, because it lowers the value at risk and
  makes C the right leg to ship first for reasons beyond "it is least sensitive".

---

## 2. The invalidation substrate — measured, and stronger than the card assumes

### 2.1 The engine seam sees every write, and it is not a call-site list

`IObjectQL.registerMiddleware` hands each middleware an `OperationContext`
(`objectql/src/engine.ts:1842`):

```ts
export interface OperationContext {
  object: string;
  operation: 'find' | 'findOne' | 'insert' | 'update' | 'delete' | 'count' | 'aggregate';
  ast?: QueryAST; data?: any; options?: any; context?: ExecutionContext; result?: any;
}
```

**Measured:** `plugin-security` already uses exactly this as an invalidation trigger, and its
docblock already argues the case this design needs (`security-plugin.ts:820-844`, `:986-993`):

- the epoch bump is the **first statement in the middleware, ahead of the `isSystem` bypass**, so
  a seeder, a package publish and the auto-org-admin grant all invalidate;
- `metadata.changed` also bumps it, because *a permission set can be declared in metadata*, so a
  Studio edit is a permission change with no row written.

**Measured, and this is the part that makes the seam decisive:** better-auth does not bypass it.
`plugin-auth/src/objectql-adapter.ts:689-691` routes better-auth's own adapter straight through
the engine:

```ts
insert: async (m, d, o) => e.insert(m, d, await asAttributedSystem(o)),
update: async (m, d, o) => e.update(m, d, await asAttributedSystem(o)),
delete: async (m, q)    => e.delete(m, await asAttributedSystem(q)),
```

So membership changes, bans, session revocation and org-role changes — everything better-auth
writes — are visible at one seam this process already owns.

**Why this matters on the AI-safety axis specifically:** a *call-site list* of "places that must
remember to invalidate" is a permanent maintenance obligation, and the failure mode when a new
grant path forgets is silent over-permission. A *seam* cannot be forgotten, because writing
through the engine is the only way to write at all. This is the "declared = enforced" shape:
a new capability-granting path physically cannot skip the invalidation.

### 2.2 Where the seam is **not** precise enough — stated, not designed past

For `insert`, `opCtx.data` carries the row. For **`update`/`delete` expressed as a `where`**, the
affected `user_id` / `organization_id` is frequently **not derivable without reading the row
back**. A design that assumes it can compute "whose cache entry does this write touch" from the
`OperationContext` is assuming something the seam does not provide.

⇒ **Ruled into this design: object-level (coarse) invalidation is the baseline.** Any write to a
watched object retires the whole cache for that leg. That is what `plugin-security` already does
(`writeEpoch++`, any write retires every entry), it is un-missable, and its only cost is
cache-effectiveness under write load. **Fine-grained keyed invalidation is a later optimization
and must not be the starting point** — see Fork 1 (§8).

### 2.3 The settings change bus already exists and is unused by the localization cache

**Measured:** `SettingsService` already has a synchronous in-process change bus —
`subscribe(namespace, handler)` (`settings-service.ts:1435`), `emitChange(...)` (`:767`), fired
from the write path (`:1708`) and from `bindEngine` (`:621`). Leg C's primary invalidation
trigger therefore requires **no new mechanism at all**; it requires a subscription.

⚠️ One measured constraint that decides its shape: the event is
`{ namespace, key, scope, action, at }` — **no tenant discriminator**. A handler cannot know
which tenant's entry to drop. ⇒ **drop the whole `localization` bucket on any `localization`
event.** Over-invalidation is the safe direction here and the cheap one; a surgical handler
would be inventing a tenant id the event does not carry.

---

## 3. Multi-node — the measurement that forces the design

The card asks for the multi-node story to be stated explicitly and for a pick-and-argue between
"per-process cache + TTL bound" and "an invalidation bus". **The measurement removes the fork
for grants and grants it for the others.** Three measured facts:

1. **The only shipped cross-node channel is `IPubSub`, and it is at-most-once.**
   `service-cluster-redis/src/pubsub.ts:78-92`, in its own words: *"Redis pub/sub is
   **at-most-once** — there is no delivery guarantee to subscribers and no replay for a node that
   was down or slow at publish time. This is acceptable **only** for events that are pure
   cache-invalidation hints, never the source of truth."* `content/docs/kernel/cluster.mdx` §4.2
   confirms at the contract level: *"No shipped driver provides `at-least-once` yet."*

2. **The one channel in production use is `metadata.changed`**, bridged by
   `MetadataClusterBridgePlugin` (`service-cluster/src/metadata-cluster-bridge-plugin.ts`), which
   **silently returns when no `cluster` service is registered** — the default composition.

3. **Row-level authorization writes have no cross-node channel today at all.** `writeEpoch++`
   fires on writes *this process's* middleware sees. Another node's grant revocation is invisible.
   That is harmless today only because the thing it guards dies with the request.

The consequences, which are the load-bearing multi-node claims of this design:

- **A bus cannot be the correctness mechanism for grants.** A dropped message on an at-most-once
  transport is an escalation window with **no upper bound**. ⇒ **The TTL is not a convenience and
  not a backstop for "paths we missed" — it is the only bound that survives the transport's own
  stated guarantee.** This is the strongest available argument for the card's ruled direction, and
  it is a measurement rather than a preference.
- **A bus is still worth adding**, as a *latency* improvement to the typical case: it moves the
  usual convergence from "one TTL" to "one network hop". It should be a **new channel on the
  existing bus** (`authz.invalidated`), following the `MetadataClusterBridgePlugin` shape exactly
  — never a new transport, never a new dependency.
- **The shipped default has no cluster service**, so the default configuration must be correct
  with no bus present. ⇒ per-process cache + TTL bound is the baseline; the bus is an optional
  tightening that lowers the *typical* window, never the *worst-case* one.
- ⚠️ **A silently-absent bridge is security-relevant here in a way it is not for metadata.** For
  metadata a missed event costs a stale schema until reload and loses no data — its own doc says
  so. For grants it costs a permission honoured past its revocation. A mechanism whose absence is
  logged at `debug` is precisely the shape of #4785 (a config that silently disabled a control).
  ⇒ **Required: a loud boot-time posture statement** when a grants cache is enabled with a
  non-zero TTL and no invalidation bus is registered. Not a refusal — a deployment may accept the
  TTL as its whole bound — but it must be *stated*, not discovered.

---

## 4. Per-leg design

Ordering below is the card's ruled order (low-sensitivity first), which is also the order in
which the invalidation contracts get progressively harder to write.

### Leg C — localization (ship first)

- **What is cached:** the **successful** outcome of `resolveLocalizationContext`. The failure-only
  cache (#10221) stays exactly as it is; this widens it to success, which is the thing #10221
  deliberately refused.
- **Key:** extend the existing table rather than adding a second one —
  `WeakMap(ql instance) → Map("tenantId|userId")`, the shape already at
  `resolve-authz-context.ts:709`. Keying on the `ql` instance is what keeps two environments in
  one process from seeing each other's answer; that property is already argued in the existing
  docblock and must be preserved.
- **Invalidation, primary:** `settings.subscribe('localization', ...)` → clear the whole bucket
  (§2.3).
- **Invalidation, backstop:** engine-seam write to `sys_setting`. Needed because the resolver's
  own fallback path reads `sys_setting` **directly** (`:806-816`), so a write that bypasses
  `SettingsService` — a seeder, a direct engine write — would emit no service event.
- **TTL:** short, configurable to zero. 30s is defensible and has two shipped precedents in this
  repo (`hostnameCacheTtlMs = 30_000` in `rest-server.ts:812`, and #10221's own
  `LOCALIZATION_FAILURE_CACHE_TTL_MS`). The value at risk is a timezone/locale/currency.
- ⭐ **Re-measured, as the card instructed:** the card says the dogfood read-after-write pin is
  satisfied by invalidation-on-write. **It is — and it is sharper than the card states.** Measured
  in `packages/qa/dogfood/test/analytics-timezone.dogfood.test.ts`: the write is a real
  `PUT /api/settings/localization`, the read is a **separate HTTP request**, and both run in **one
  process, sequentially awaited**. Therefore:
  - a **synchronous, in-process** invalidation on the settings event satisfies it;
  - a **TTL alone does not** — 30s far exceeds the inter-request gap;
  - an **asynchronous or deferred** invalidation does not reliably satisfy it either.
  ⇒ **That test already is the acceptance test for "write-invalidation primary" on leg C.** It goes
  red exactly when the primary mechanism is missing and the timer is doing the work. Keep it
  unchanged and unweakened; it is free coverage of the property that matters most.

### Leg D — metadata (ship second)

- **What is cached:** the `sys_metadata` overlay read inside `getMetaItems` — the 2–4 reads and
  ≥2 sequential legs measured in §1.
- **Key:** `(environmentId, canonical type, packageId, organizationId, previewDrafts)` **plus an
  epoch**. The epoch is the card's "registry-epoch keyed": bump on (i) any engine-seam write to
  `sys_metadata`, and (ii) any `metadata.changed` watch event.
- **Multi-node: already solved for this leg.** `metadata.changed` is bridged cross-node today, and
  leg D is the one leg where an at-most-once hint is genuinely adequate — by the transport's own
  documented criterion (a missed event costs a stale schema until reload; no data loss, self-heals).
- ⚠️ **Trap that a naive implementation will hit.** `getMetaItems` is not a pure read: its
  overlay-hydration branch **registers overlay rows back into the SchemaRegistry** (see the
  `#4432` comment at `protocol.ts:5993-6001`, and `:159`). A cache that skips the read also skips
  that registration, and the symptom is not a stale answer — it is a registry that stops being
  populated. ⇒ **Cache the merged post-hydration result, or keep hydration outside the cached
  path and prove it idempotent.** Naming this is most of why leg D deserved a design pass.
- ⚠️ **Negative caching is where the win is, and it is the entry most in need of the epoch.** The
  empty result is what triggers the alt-type retry, so caching "empty" is the bulk of the saving —
  and a newly published overlay must appear promptly. The epoch, not the TTL, is what makes that
  correct; a TTL-only leg D would make publish-visibility a timer.
- **TTL:** short, configurable to zero, as a bound on the same at-most-once transport.

### Leg B — grants (ship third; the one the card is really about)

- **What is cached:** the `UserAuthzGrants` envelope from `resolveUserAuthzGrants`.
- **Watched objects** (derived by reading §3–§7 of the resolver): `sys_member`,
  `sys_user_position`, `sys_user_permission_set`, `sys_position`, `sys_position_permission_set`,
  `sys_permission_set`, `sys_user`. Plus `metadata.changed` for declared permission sets.
  ⚠️ **`sys_session` is deliberately NOT in this set** — see the measured reason under leg A.
- **Invalidation triggers, per mutation path:**

  | mutation | reaches the seam as | retires |
  |---|---|---|
  | grant / revoke a permission set to a user | write to `sys_user_permission_set` | leg B, all entries |
  | role change (better-auth org role) | write to `sys_member` (via the ObjectQL adapter) | leg B, all entries |
  | auto-org-admin reconcile | write to `sys_user_permission_set` (system write — caught because the bump precedes the `isSystem` bypass) | leg B, all entries |
  | position assign / deactivate | `sys_user_position` / `sys_position` | leg B, all entries |
  | permission-set edit, deactivate, or `system_permissions`/`tab_permissions` change | `sys_permission_set` | leg B, all entries |
  | permission set **declared in metadata** | `metadata.changed` | leg B, all entries |
  | `ai_access` toggle | `sys_user` | leg B, all entries |
  | settings write | *not a leg-B trigger* | — |

- ⭐ **Three correctness constraints that a naive keying gets wrong. These are the substance of
  this leg.**

  **B.1 — The answer is a function of the clock, and caching freezes it.**
  Validity windows (ADR-0091) are evaluated at resolution time: `isGrantActive(row, nowMs)` is
  applied to `sys_member`, `sys_user_position` and `sys_user_permission_set` rows, and `nowMs` is
  taken once per resolution (`:383`). A cached envelope therefore **freezes a validity decision**:
  a grant whose `valid_until` passes *during* the TTL keeps resolving until the entry expires.
  No write occurs at that boundary, so **no write-invalidation can ever catch it** — the entire
  primary mechanism is blind to this class by construction.
  ⇒ **Required:** an entry must carry the **earliest upcoming validity boundary** among the rows
  it consulted, and expire at `min(ttl, nextBoundary)`. Without it, "expires at T" silently
  becomes "expires at T rounded up by the TTL", and ADR-0091's fail-closed promise quietly
  acquires a tolerance. I have not found this stated anywhere in the #10757 lineage.

  **B.2 — Seeds are part of the answer, and their order is contractual.**
  `seedPermissions` (API-key scopes) and `seedEmail` enter the envelope
  (`grants.permissions = [...opts.seedPermissions]`, then set names appended), and the existing
  golden asserts **array order** deliberately. Two options: put the seeds in the key, or cache the
  **seedless** envelope and apply seeds outside it. The second is better (one entry per
  `(userId, tenantId)` instead of one per key-scope combination) **but it is only sound because
  seeding is a pure prepend**, which must be *pinned*, not assumed. Note also that a seeded
  API-key principal suppresses the `sys_user` read entirely (`needsUserRow` at `:365`) — so the
  seedless entry issues a read the seeded path would not have. That is a *query-multiset*
  difference the existing golden will notice.

  **B.3 — `org_user_ids` depends on OTHER users' rows.**
  The fellow-org peer list is `sys_member {organization_id} limit 1000` (`:370`). It changes when
  **any** user's membership in that organization changes. ⇒ invalidation on a `sys_member` write
  must retire **every entry for that organization**, not the written user's entry. This is the
  single most likely place for a "fine-grained invalidation" optimization to introduce a silent
  bug, and it is a second reason coarse invalidation is the right baseline.

- ⭐ **Two call sites that must bypass the cache.** `resolveUserAuthzGrants` has 17 call sites
  across 12 packages (measured); two of them are wrong to serve from cache:
  - **`plugin-security/src/explain-engine.ts:473`** — the permission *explainer*. This is the tool
    an administrator uses to verify that a revocation took effect. An explainer answering from
    cache would explain a state that no longer exists, and would do it at exactly the moment
    someone is checking. ⇒ **`explain` takes a force-fresh path.**
  - **`service-automation/src/plugin.ts:812`** — `runAs:'user'` automation runs. These are not
    request-shaped and can be long-lived; they must not pin an envelope.
- **TTL:** the security-sensitive number. The card rules "order of seconds, default conservative".
  Recommendation and the one number to confirm: **default `0` (off) for leg B specifically**, with
  a supported non-zero range in the low seconds. Rationale: legs C and D deliver real latency with
  a defensible story; leg B is where the escalation window lives, and shipping it *on* by default
  makes every existing deployment absorb a posture change it did not ask for. A deployment that
  wants it turns it on knowingly — which is also what makes the boot-time posture statement (§3)
  meaningful rather than noise.
- **Depends on #10348-C landing.** See §6.

### Leg A — session (ship last, and not in the form the card sketches)

⭐ **Measured blocker: the two mechanisms #10757's direction 1 names are already ruled out, one of
them by a closed decision with landed pins.**

- **`secondaryStorage` — closed decision.** #4785 (*"where is the session of record?"*) is
  **closed as completed** via merged PR #5101, fixing the answer: **it is always `sys_session`, the
  database**. The reasoning is recorded in `plugin-auth/src/secondary-storage.ts:22-38`: handing
  better-auth a `secondaryStorage` moves the session of record into it —
  `internalAdapter.createSession` skips the `sys_session` row and `findSession` answers from the
  cached snapshot without consulting the database — while ObjectStack revokes sessions **by
  writing that row** (`enforceSessionControls` / `enforceConcurrentCap` stamp `revoked_at` plus a
  past `expires_at`, ADR-0069 D4). The result is that idle-timeout, absolute-max and
  concurrent-cap revocation **silently stop taking effect**.
  It is pinned. `plugin-auth/src/session-of-record.test.ts` carries, by name:
  `'opting into cacheSecondaryStorage empties sys_session and makes idle timeout inert'`,
  `'option C (dual-write) is not reachable through config — asking for it changes nothing'`, and
  `'the DEFAULT composition refuses to boot with a secondaryStorage rather than degrading
  quietly'`. Its header states the discipline this whole design should borrow: *"every test here
  asserts the END of the chain, not the middle: a request that carries a real session cookie stops
  being authenticated. Asserting only that the row was stamped would re-create the exact blind
  spot."*
- **`cookieCache` — same ground, no guard.** **Measured with a positive control:** `cookieCache`
  has **zero hits repo-wide** (`git grep` exit 1, 0 lines; the control on the same instrument
  returns 10 hits), so it is genuinely unconfigured. But it is a *different better-auth key
  reaching the same architecture*: it answers `getSession` from a signed cookie snapshot without
  reading `sys_session`, so a session revoked by writing the row keeps authenticating for the
  cookie's TTL. ⇒ **#10757's direction 1, as written, is not available without re-opening a closed
  ruling.** ⚠️ And worth recording on its own: the `secondaryStorage` door is boot-refused while
  the `cookieCache` door is unguarded — the same rejected architecture reachable through a config
  key nothing pins. That is a gap in the guard, not a gap in the ruling.

⇒ **What leg A becomes:**

- **A1 — the `customSession` enrichment (3 of leg A's ~5 reads).** ⭐ **Do not design a cache for
  this. #10348-C deletes it.** Option C (ruled 2026-08-24) removes the id-shaped judges from
  `auth-manager.ts` and sends both call sites to `resolve-authz-context.ts`. Post-C the enrichment
  is *the same derivation as leg B*, so **leg B's cache serves it, with leg B's single invalidation
  contract.** Designing A1 separately would create a second cached derivation of the same fact —
  the exact drift shape #10348 exists to end.
- **A2 — better-auth's own `sys_session` + `sys_user` read.** This is the half #4785 fenced.
  **Out of scope for this design.** It is not a cache-design surface; it is a
  ruled-decision surface, and reaching it means re-opening #4785 Option B *with* the revocation
  rewrite that option always required. Proposed as a decision card, not an implementation card (§7).
- ⭐ **Measured reason `sys_session` must stay out of leg B's watched set.**
  `enforceSessionControls` **writes** `last_activity_at` on a throttled cadence — *once a minute
  per active session* (`auth-manager.ts:5771-5776`). Under coarse object-level invalidation, that
  write would retire the entire grants cache roughly every minute on any deployment with idle
  timeout configured. `sys_session` does not feed the grants envelope, so excluding it is free —
  but only if someone notices, and the natural instinct ("sessions are authz, watch them") gets it
  wrong. This is also a general warning for Fork 1: **a watched object with a background write
  cadence silently converts a cache into a non-cache.**

---

## 5. Config surface

- ⭐ **Deployment config (`OS_*` env), never a settings row.** Two reasons, one of them measured:
  1. Settings live in `sys_setting`, which **leg C caches**. A staleness bound read through a
     cached path is a bootstrap hazard — the knob that governs the cache would be served by the
     cache.
  2. It matches the direction #11663 is being ruled on for operator-level configuration
     ("operator-level admin comes from deployment config, never from business data"), and the
     existing settings service already models env as outranking every persisted scope
     (`effectiveEnvOverride`), so the two channels do not fight.
- **One variable per leg**, so the low-sensitivity legs can ship enabled while leg B stays off.
  Each accepts `0` = off, and `0` must be a *real* path, not a degenerate TTL (see pin 7).
- Registered in `content/docs/deployment/environment-variables.mdx`, the canonical table.
- ⛔ **Spec-seat leg, not taken here:** if the invalidation event or a cache-posture value needs a

## 7. Test and pin plan

The existing batch-equivalence golden discipline extends naturally, and the harness is reusable:
`makeRecordingQl` is **exported** from `resolve-authz-context.batch-equivalence.test.ts` and
already records the query multiset *and* counts real legs. ⚠️ Cross-package test imports are gated
(`check:cross-package-test-inputs`), so a pin outside `packages/core` needs the repo's `.testkit.ts`
convention (8 such files exist today) rather than importing the test file.

1. **Identity — cached ≡ uncached.** For each fixture in the existing 11-fixture matrix: resolve
   twice; deep-equal **including array order**; and assert the second resolution issued **zero**
   reads. Both halves are needed — equality alone passes on a cache that never caches.
2. ⭐ **Revocation — the pin that catches the failure that matters.** Populate the cache, revoke a
   capability **through the engine** (the same seam a real revoke uses), resolve again, and assert
   **the capability is absent**, with **no clock advance**.
   ⚠️ It must assert the *absence of the capability*, not "the cache was cleared" — a
   clear-then-repopulate-from-a-stale-read implementation passes the second and fails the first.
   This is `session-of-record.test.ts`'s own discipline ("assert the END of the chain, not the
   middle"), which is the right precedent because it was written after exactly this blind spot.
   The implementation card **must** ablate write-invalidation and report the observed direction.
3. **Validity boundary (pins B.1).** A grant whose `valid_until` falls *inside* the TTL stops
   resolving at the boundary, not at TTL expiry. No write occurs, so this pin is the only thing
   that can catch it.
4. **Peer membership (pins B.3).** User X's envelope must change when user **Y**'s `sys_member` row
   in the same organization is written.
5. **Seed isolation (pins B.2).** Two callers with different `seedPermissions` never see each
   other's envelope; ordering matches the existing golden; and the seeded-API-key path's suppressed
   `sys_user` read is preserved in the query multiset.
6. **Explain path.** `explain-engine` observes a revocation immediately.
7. ⭐ **Zero means off.** With the cache configured to `0`, the query multiset is **byte-identical
   to today's golden**. This is what makes "configurable to zero" an escape hatch a deployment can
   rely on rather than a claim in a docblock.
8. **Leg C.** `analytics-timezone.dogfood.test.ts` unchanged and unweakened — it is already the
   leg-C acceptance test (§4, leg C).
9. **Multi-node.** Two cache instances plus a bus double: a write on node 1 retires node 2's entry;
   and **with the bus absent, node 2 still converges by TTL** — the pin that proves the bound
   exists independently of the transport.

## 8. Forks — where a real choice remains

### Fork 1 — invalidation granularity for leg B: coarse vs keyed

- **A. Coarse (recommended).** Any write to a watched object retires the whole leg-B cache.
- **B. Keyed.** Retire only entries for the affected user / organization.

**Real business need:** the pull is cloud#1521's fixed per-request cost. Coarse delivers it on
read-heavy traffic, which is the measured shape (a Console cold load fires 27 API calls). Keyed
only wins on write-heavy tenants, and nobody has measured one. **Long-term soundness:** coarse has
one rule; keyed needs a correct write→entry mapping that §2.2 shows the seam does not supply, and
§B.3 shows is counter-intuitive for `org_user_ids`. **AI-safety:** decisive for coarse — keyed
invalidation is the shape where a wrong mapping over-permits *silently*, and it is exactly the kind
of mapping an AI-authored change extends without noticing `org_user_ids`. **Startup scope:** coarse
is less code and no new concepts. ⇒ **A, and keyed is not a follow-up to schedule — it is a
follow-up to justify with a measurement first.**

### Fork 2 — multi-node: TTL-only vs adding an `authz.invalidated` channel

- **A. TTL-only** (per-process caches, no cross-node signal).
- **B. TTL + a new channel on the existing at-most-once bus (recommended).**

**Real business need:** cloud runs more than one instance, so under A every grant change costs a
full TTL on every node that did not serve the write. **Long-term soundness:** B reuses a shipped
transport and a shipped bridge pattern; it adds no dependency and no new failure mode, *because*
the TTL still bounds the worst case — B is strictly a narrowing of the typical window. **AI-safety:**
B is safe only if nobody is allowed to read it as the correctness mechanism; the design must say
in the code, at the channel, that a missed message is expected and the TTL is the contract.
**Startup scope:** B is small precisely because `MetadataClusterBridgePlugin` already shows the
shape. ⇒ **B, with the §3 boot-time posture statement as a non-optional part of it.**

### Fork 3 — leg A's remaining half (better-auth's own session read)

- **A. Leave it (recommended for this card).** Session reads stay uncached; #4785's ruling stands.
- **B. Re-open #4785 Option B** — session of record moves to the cache, ADR-0069 D4's revocation is
  rewritten to invalidate the cache as well as write the row.

**Real business need:** it is ~2 of a request's reads after legs B/C/D land — the smallest remaining
share. **Long-term soundness:** B requires an ADR revision and makes revocation a two-place
consistency problem; #4785 already analysed it and the maintainer already chose A. **AI-safety:**
#4785's own words — "撤销从一次写变成两处一致性，AI 生成的新管控极易只写一半". **Startup scope:**
reopening a settled architectural decision for the smallest remaining win is the definition of
scope diffusion. ⇒ **A. If B is ever wanted, it is a decision card that re-opens #4785, never a
performance card.**

### Fork 4 — the one number to confirm

Leg B's **default** TTL. This design recommends **`0` (off by default)** with a supported low-seconds
range, for the reason in §4 (leg B). The card rules "short, default conservative"; `0` is the most
conservative reading, and it makes the deployment's acceptance of a staleness window explicit.
**If the maintainer wants leg B on by default, that is a posture change this design does not
assume** — it is named here rather than chosen quietly.
